name: Santee Sioux Nation
land_summary: After the 1862 war in Minnesota, the Santee Dakota were imprisoned or forced onto the Crow Creek reservation in Dakota Territory. In 1866 they were moved again, to the Niobrara country in northeast Nebraska, where an executive order reserved four townships for them near the mouth of the Niobrara River. Some families soon left to homestead along the Big Sioux River, founding the Flandreau community. Much later, the Gavins Point Dam on the Missouri took about 593 acres near the village of Santee and about 414 acres on Niobrara Island, and Congress eventually passed a compensation act covering the Santee and the Yankton. Today the reservation lies along the Missouri near the mouth of the Niobrara.

timeline.event: The Santee are moved from Crow Creek to Nebraska, and an executive order reserves four townships for them on the Niobrara.

sources.name: American Presidency Project, Executive Order of February 27, 1866 (Niobrara Reserve)
SD State Archives, Indian Archives Project, Crow Creek Agency
Flandreau Santee Sioux Tribe, About Us

notes: This draft is weak and needs nation input. Only one dated entry could be double-sourced, below the required 3 to 8. No Santee Sioux Nation website could be reached; the listed domain returned a generic page. No independent source was found for allotment or later openings of the Santee reservation, for its current acreage and trust/fee mix, or for its county (Knox County is likely but was not sourced). The summary leaves these out rather than guess. The Gavins Point figures come from Senate Report 106-367. Senate Report 111-357 gives 1,007 acres in total, which matches. The compensation act (Pub. L. 107-331, 2002) is documented only in Senate reports, so it is undated. The 1863 removal year to Crow Creek is widely cited but was not stated in the sources reviewed. A History Nebraska page on the Santee should be sought.
